newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - ABARE cuts Australian 1996/97 lead output.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - ABARE cuts Australian 1996/97 lead output.

text.p: Australian lead mine output is seen three percent higher to 520,000 tonnes in the 1996/97 year, but is down on the June forecast of 530,000, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE).
ABARE said in its September quarterly report that lead prices are forecast to rise over calendar 1996 and also in 1997, with stocks falling as a result of world lead consumption exceeding production.
The government advisory body said the higher price and output is expected to boost Australia's lead export earnings by 16.7 percent to A$532 million in the year to June 30, 1997.

The growth in Australia's lead output is due to the start of the McArthur River base metals mine in the Northern Territory this year and higher output at Mount Isa, Queensland, both mines are operated by MIM Holdings Ltd, ABARE said.
"The forecast lead price rises follow increases in 1994 and 1995, and reflect a further tightening of the world lead market," ABARE said.

The bureau estimates the lead price to average US$880 per tonne or $40 per pound (lb) in calendar 1997, compared with a forecast of $816 per tonne or $37 per lb in 1996. The lead price closed at $785 in London Metal Exchange trading on Monday.
ABARE said lead stocks are forecast to decline by 9.1 percent to 4.1 weeks of consumption by the end of 1996, and to around four weeks by the end of 1997.

"Given the low stocks, spot prices for lead can be expected to exceed US$900/tonne in periods of peak demand (such as at the end of the northern hemisphere summer and winter, when there is high demand for replacement batteries) in response to concerns regarding short term regional shortages," ABARE said.
The bureau forecast world production to rise 3.2 percent to 5.68 million tonnes for calendar 1997, while consumption is seen up 2.3 percent to 5.78 million in 1997 from 5.65 million.
ABARE said the higher world lead output mainly reflects reactivations and expansions of existing mines in Canada, the United States, Europe and increases in Australian production.
The bureau said almost all new lead production will come from zinc-lead ore bodies in which zinc is the dominant metal.

The growth in 1997 lead consumption is driven by steady growth in industrial production in Western Europe, Canada and the United States, and the relatively strong economic growth in China, Malaysia, Thailand, South Korea and Indonesia.
